pr_body:
Profiling showed the compiler was producing rotate_left()
function calls in this hot path for what should compile down to
just a few trivial instructions.

Commit a1e92eee3 removed the inline from this macro-style
function, which seems suspect, but my brief testing reintroducing
the inline here on my Arch system w/gcc 11.1.0 and whatever flags
the meson build system uses still produced a rotate_left()
function substantially harming siphash24 performance vs. an
explicit ROTATE_LEFT() macro.

I don't know if this should be considered a compiler bug or
something wrong about how meson is configuring the builds, but I
think leaving the inline decision for such perf sensitive trivial
operations up to build-time chance/compiler optimizer heuristics
just doesn't make sense.

This commit makes it a traditional macro, which seems perfectly
correct to me for this kind of thing.

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/20572
pr_comments:
> Have you tried always_inline attribute?

Negative, take a look at how many times `always_inline` occurs in the entire systemd git repo.

The macro form is guaranteed to be inlined since the C preprocessor is just an automated copy and paste, I don't see a good reason to not use it in this case.  But I don't have an allergy to macros in C code.
i'd be fine with this being a macro, but should have comments, as to why
was your build with optimization on?
It's clear how to correct this and I think it's an obviously right thing to do, but closing for seeming lack of interest after a long period of falling off my radar.

issue_context.title: commit a1e92eee3 significantly regresses siphash performance when compiler doesn't inline rotate_left()
issue_context.body:
The commit message for a1e92eee3 refers to a review comment by Lennart saying not to use static inline outside of headers (https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/11397#discussion_r247560335).  Then this commit goes and cargo cults the rule throughout the code without considering the potential consequences for when the compiler decides not to inline.

If we're not supposed to inline for some reason (I suspect it's because compilers have started overriding/ignoring these hints), even in scenarios where it's damn obvious that static inline was being used in place of what would clearly be a macro in years past, I think we should consider replacing those inlines with macros instead of blindly dropping the inline.

Perf difference for `journalctl --verify` in my tests with the compiler uninlined rotate_left() vs. replacing it with a macro ensuring it's inlined is 6.42seconds vs. 5.606seconds, 13% faster, in a process which wastes the vast majority of its real time elsewhere.  

At the very least more attention should be paid to ensuring optimal hash performance is consistently delivered by systemd builds, considering how many aspects incorporate the shared hash infra.
comments:
I tripped over this while down an unrelated rabbithole compariing `jio verify hashed-objects` performance vs. a `journalctl --verify` modified to only perform the data object hashing from the first verify iteration, since that's all jio is doing.  After seeing the `rotate_left()` function in the profiles I reran some of the graph-producing runs from my unrelated work with `rotate_left()` macroified since it was still convenient and it seemed unfair for my comparisons to have such a crippled `journalctl --verify`, they clearly show the runtime difference so will attach them here.

The width of the activity portion in the graphs reflects the runtime duration for the process.   These graphs are sampled at 60hz producing a 1px vertical bar per sample... so 60 horizontal pixels represents a second of real wall-clock time.  These runs are both cached, as in the journals being verified are already 100% in the page cache so no IO Wait.

rotate_left() as a function:
![](https://pengaru.com/~vc/tmp/jio-vmon/sd-v248-verify-data-objects-only-cache-08.26.21-03%3A00%3A15-0.png)

As a macro:
![](https://pengaru.com/~vc/tmp/jio-vmon/sd-v248-verify-data-objects-macroify-cache-08.29.21-18%3A29%3A54-0.png)

I mention this in the commit @ https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/20573, but will repeat it here for posterity:
Testing with the inline restored for `rotate_left()` the compiler appeared to still be producing a `rotate_left()` function for some reason, hence a macroify PR instead of restoring the inline.

Note this is specifically an issue for when the compiler isn't optimizing.  So if you're running a debug build for instance, this macro currently becomes a function call in a very hot path.  I've since confirmed that if I configure meson for a release build here this is not an issue, but I don't think we want to severely penalize the default debug build like this.  Though in that vein one could argue sipround() also shouldn't be a separate function either...

I find it odd that there's so much reliance on assuming that optimizers will ensure such things are kept fast.

My $.02 is that we should be making a good-faith effort to ensure even less aggressively optimized/debuggable builds have such hot code paths kept fast when it's not a big effort or addition of technical debt, and doesn't significantly harm debuggability or legibility.

Consider all the CI stuff that runs tests using debuggable builds and how much time/energy is burned on those.  The ROTATE_LEFT hash example made a significant difference, it should just be a macro, in *all* builds.  And when developers are wasting their time testing/reproducing stuff against test datasets, their time shouldn't be wasted any more than necessary waiting for pointlessly made-slow code to run in debuggable builds that are already inherently slower.  It's unclear to me how we got here, but it's annoying.

Closing for lack of interest.
